cards: Revenue
The value of what was sold in a period, recorded when earned, whether or not cash has arrived.
Accrual principle
Record revenue when earned and expenses when they help earn it, not when cash moves.
Deferred revenue
Cash received for goods or services not yet delivered. A liability.
Retained earnings
All past profits kept in the business. A source of funding, not a pile of cash.
EBIT
Earnings before interest and tax. Operating profit, independent of how the firm is financed.
Capex
Spending on assets used for more than a year. Goes on the balance sheet and is depreciated.
Opex
Spending used up within the period. Charged to profit immediately.
Working capital
Money tied up in inventory and receivables, less what is owed to suppliers.
Overtrading
A profitable firm running out of cash because growth absorbs working capital.
Consolidated statements
Accounts covering a parent company and all its subsidiaries.
Capital work-in-progress
Money spent on plants and lines not yet operating. A sign of capacity about to start.
Fixed cost
A cost that does not change with output over a range, such as rent or salaries.
Contribution margin
Price minus variable cost. What each unit puts towards fixed costs and profit.
Activity-based costing
Allocating overhead by the activities that cause it, such as set-ups or change orders.
Variance analysis
Splitting the gap between budget and actual into causes, such as volume and price.
Hard benefit
A benefit that lowers cash spending or brings in cash. Soft benefits free time or reduce risk.

formulas: % change in quantity ÷ % change in price
Size below 1 is inelastic: a price rise raises revenue.
Break-even volume loss for a price cut
Match a rival's cut only if you would otherwise lose more than this.
Each doubling of cumulative output cuts unit cost by a fixed %
R² is the share of variation explained.
cards: Movement along versus shift
A change in the product's own price moves along a curve. Anything else shifts the curve.
Inelastic demand
Quantity changes proportionally less than price. Few substitutes or high switching costs.
Complement
A product whose use raises demand for another, such as robots and fixtures.
Opportunity cost
The value of the best alternative given up.
Sunk cost
Money already spent that cannot be recovered. Irrelevant to future decisions.
Price discrimination
Charging different customers different prices, for example through versions or segments.
Barrier to entry
Anything that stops new firms competing away profit: scale, switching costs, patents, brand.
Oligopoly
A market with few sellers whose decisions affect each other.
Dominant strategy
A choice that is best whatever the other player does.
Nash equilibrium
A set of choices where no player can do better by changing alone.
Prisoner's dilemma
Each player's best individual choice leads to a result worse for all.
Base rate
How common the thing you are looking for is. Rare events make most alerts false.
Survivorship bias
Drawing conclusions only from cases that passed a selection, ignoring those that did not.
p-value
The chance of a result at least this extreme if nothing had really changed.
Type I and Type II errors
Type I: a false alarm. Type II: a missed real effect.
Confounding variable
A third factor that drives both things you observe moving together.
Selection bias
The group studied differs from the group you want to conclude about, often because it volunteered.

formulas: C is next year's cash flow.
PV of future cash flows − Initial investment
The discount rate at which NPV = 0
EBITDA − Tax, where Tax = rate × (EBITDA − Depreciation)
Risk-free rate + Beta × Equity risk premium

EBIT × (1 − tax) + Depreciation − Capex − Increase in working capital
cards: Discount rate
The return available on the best alternative use of money at similar risk.
Net present value
How much richer a project makes the firm, in today's money.
Why IRR can mislead
It ignores scale and timing. For mutually exclusive projects, follow NPV.
Incremental cash flow
Cash flow with the project minus cash flow without it.
Depreciation tax shield
The tax saved because depreciation reduces taxable profit.
Specific risk
Risk peculiar to one company. It can be diversified away, so investors are not paid for it.
Market risk
Risk shared by all firms, such as recessions. It cannot be diversified away.
Beta
How sensitive a share is to movements in the whole market.
WACC
The blended return a company's lenders and shareholders require.
Hurdle rate
The minimum return a company demands of projects. Often set above WACC.
Enterprise value
The value of a company's operations to all investors, before subtracting net debt.
EV/EBITDA
A valuation multiple that compares firms regardless of how much debt they carry.
Leverage
Using debt. It magnifies returns to shareholders in both directions.
Leveraged buyout
Buying a company mostly with debt, improving it, repaying debt and selling.
Real versus nominal
Nominal includes inflation. Real removes it. Cash flows and rate must match.
Economic profit
(Return on capital − cost of capital) × capital employed.

formulas: TAM × serviceable share = SAM. SAM × winnable share = SOM.
Price of next best alternative + Value of differences − Adoption cost
Volume needed to offset a discount
Sales and marketing cost ÷ New customers won
Revenue per customer × Gross margin ÷ Churn rate
CAC ÷ Gross profit per customer per year
(Opening ARR + Expansion − Contraction − Churn) ÷ Opening ARR
Opportunities × Deal size × Win rate ÷ Cycle length
cards: Segmentation, targeting, positioning
Divide the market, choose whom to serve, decide what to stand for.
Positioning
The place your offer holds in the customer's mind relative to alternatives.
Point of parity
Something you must match to be considered at all.
Jobs to be done
Customers hire a product to do a job. Ask what job, and what else could do it.
TAM, SAM, SOM
Total market, the part you can serve, and the share you can realistically win.
Buying centre
The group involved in a business purchase: user, influencer, economic buyer, purchaser, gatekeeper.
Economic buyer
The person who weighs your proposal against other uses of the same budget.
Value-based pricing
Setting price as a share of the measurable benefit to the customer.
Price metric
What you charge per: user, line, unit. It should rise as customer value rises.
Pocket price
What remains after all discounts, rebates and free extras.
Whole product
Everything the customer needs to get the result, including services and partners.
The chasm
The gap between visionary early adopters and pragmatists who want references.
Channel conflict
Two routes to market chasing the same customer.
Churn
The share of customers or revenue lost in a period.
Net revenue retention
What existing customers pay this year against last, including upgrades and losses.
Bookings, billings, revenue
Contracts signed, invoices issued, and service delivered. Three different numbers.

formulas: Takt time = Available time ÷ Customer demand.
Units per hour × Contribution per unit
√(2 × Annual demand × Order cost ÷ Holding cost per unit)

Daily demand × Lead time + Safety stock

Distance from mean to nearer spec limit ÷ (3 × SD)
Product of each step's first-pass yield
cards: Bottleneck
The resource with the lowest capacity. It sets the output of the whole process.
Five focusing steps
Identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat.
Drum-buffer-rope
Bottleneck sets the pace, a buffer protects it, release is tied to its consumption.
Why queues form below full capacity
Arrivals and processing vary, and idle capacity cannot be stored.
Three buffers
Variability is absorbed by inventory, capacity or time.
Pooling
Combining sources of variability so highs and lows offset.
Late differentiation
Postponing the variant decision until demand is known.
Jidoka
Building quality in by stopping when a problem occurs.
Seven wastes
Overproduction, waiting, transport, over-processing, inventory, motion, defects.
SMED
Quick changeover. It makes small batches affordable.
Cost of quality
Prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure costs.
Common versus special cause
Normal noise of a stable process versus a specific, findable cause.
DMAIC
Define, measure, analyse, improve, control.
Bullwhip effect
Order swings grow further up the supply chain.
Functional versus innovative product
Stable demand needs an efficient chain. Uncertain demand needs a responsive one.
Kraljic matrix
Purchases sorted by profit impact and supply risk: leverage, strategic, routine, bottleneck.
Total cost of ownership
Purchase price plus freight, duty, stock, quality and risk costs.

formulas: Customer keeps WTP − Price. Firm keeps Price − Cost.
Value of an acquisition to the buyer
PV of synergies − Premium paid − Integration costs
A fall of x% needs a rise of x ÷ (100 − x) to recover
cards: Strategy (Porter)
Choosing a distinct position that involves trade-offs, including what not to do.
The kernel (Rumelt)
Diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent actions.
Five forces
Rivalry, new entrants, buyer power, supplier power, substitutes.
Profit pool
How an industry's total profit is spread across the stages of its chain.
Differentiation
Raising willingness to pay by more than it costs to do so.
Stuck in the middle
Neither the lowest-cost nor clearly better. Exposed from both sides.
VRIO
A resource supports lasting advantage if valuable, rare, costly to imitate and organised for.
Switching costs
What a customer must spend to change supplier. They protect the installed base.
Counter-positioning
A new model incumbents will not copy because it would damage their own business.
Disruptive innovation
A simpler, cheaper product that starts where incumbents will not compete and improves.
Better-off test
Do businesses gain an advantage from being under one owner?
Winner's curse
The winning bidder tends to be the one who overestimated most.
Indirect network effect
More users on one side of a platform attract more on the other.
Multi-homing
Users belonging to several networks at once. It weakens winner-take-all.
Repo rate
The rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends to banks. Its main policy tool.
Natural hedge
Matching the currency of costs and revenues.

formulas: Between the seller's minimum and the buyer's maximum
No overlap means no deal on that issue alone.
Effort → Performance → Reward → Value of the reward
Motivation fails if any link is broken.
Urgency, coalition, vision, communicate, remove obstacles, short-term wins, consolidate, anchor
cards: Hygiene factors
Things like pay and policies that cause dissatisfaction when poor but do not motivate when fixed.
Self-determination
Lasting motivation comes from autonomy, competence and relatedness.
Rewarding A while hoping for B
Paying for one behaviour while wanting another, and getting what is paid for.
Psychological safety
A shared belief that it is safe to speak up, ask and admit mistakes.
Planning fallacy
Expecting a project to finish sooner and cheaper than similar ones did.
Outside view
Estimating from how similar past cases actually turned out.
Pre-mortem
Imagining the project has failed and listing why, before starting.
Star model
Strategy, structure, processes, rewards and people must fit together.
Underlying assumptions
The deepest level of culture: what people take for granted.
BATNA
Your best alternative if no agreement is reached. Your real source of power.
Anchoring
The first number mentioned pulls the outcome towards it.
Logrolling
Trading across issues the two sides value differently.
Position versus interest
What someone says they want versus why they want it.
Task-relevant maturity
How experienced a person is at a specific task. It sets how closely to manage.
Agency problem
Managers' interests can differ from those of the owners whose money they manage.
Answer first
State the recommendation at the start, then the reasons, then the evidence.

formulas: Cash in the bank ÷ Net cash burned per month
New holding = Old holding × (1 − New investors' share)
cards: Four product risks
Value, usability, feasibility and viability.
Output versus outcome
A feature shipped versus a change in customer or business results.
Product discovery
Finding out what is worth building, quickly and cheaply, before building it.
Minimum viable product
The smallest version that lets you learn the most about customers.
North-star metric
One measure that captures the value customers get from the product.
Kano basics
Features customers expect and only notice when missing.
Digital thread
Connected product and process data across design, manufacturing and service.
Why pilots do not scale
No owner, no baseline, weak foundations, unmanaged change.
Prediction machines
AI as a fall in the cost of prediction, which raises the value of data, judgement and action.
Staged autonomy
Start with suggestions reviewed by people and widen what a system may do as evidence builds.
Business model canvas
Nine blocks describing how a business creates, delivers and captures value.
Beachhead market
One narrow segment to win completely before expanding.
Unit economics
What one unit brings in, costs to deliver and costs to acquire.
Pivot
A change to one part of the business model, based on evidence.
Affordable loss
Commit only what you can lose without lasting harm.
Break-even assumption
The value of a key input at which the decision would change.
